name: Hawaiian
variety: Standard Hawaiian as used across the islands and in the revitalisation movement (Parker Jones 2018, a speaker from Hawaiʻi island), with the older description of Elbert & Pukui (1979); Niʻihau speech differs (t for k, more taps for l)
sources: Parker Jones, ʻŌiwi (2018). Hawaiian. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 48(1), 103-115.
Elbert, Samuel H. & Pukui, Mary Kawena (1979). Hawaiian Grammar. Honolulu: University Press of Hawaii.
Pukui, Mary Kawena & Elbert, Samuel H. (1986). Hawaiian Dictionary, revised and enlarged edition. Honolulu: University of Hawaii Press.
Schütz, Albert J. (1981). A reanalysis of the Hawaiian vowel system. Oceanic Linguistics 20(1), 1-43.
Schütz, Albert J. (1994). The Voices of Eden: A History of Hawaiian Language Studies. Honolulu: University of Hawaii Press.
Parker Jones, ʻŌiwi (2010). A Computational Phonology and Morphology of Hawaiian. DPhil thesis, University of Oxford.
Murphy, Kelly Erin (2013). Melodies of Hawaiʻi: The Relationship Between Hawaiʻi Creole English and ʻŌlelo Hawaiʻi Prosody. PhD thesis, University of Calgary.
Davidson, Lisa (2021). Effects of word position and flanking vowel on the implementation of glottal stop: evidence from Hawaiian. Journal of Phonetics 88.
contrasts: short versus long vowels: Kona 'leeward' versus kōna 'his, hers', hui 'club' versus hūi 'halloo', pela 'mattress' versus pēla 'bail'
glottal stop versus its absence, also word-initially: ʻaka 'laugh' versus aka 'shadow', kou 'your' versus koʻu 'my'
eight consonants only; no voicing contrast, no sibilants, no contrast of t and k or of w and v
diphthongs versus sequences of two syllables (loina with a diphthong, moena with two syllables)
allophony: /k/ varies with [t]; [k] is usual in the standard, [t] on Niʻihau and in some chant and older speech

/w/ varies between [w], [v] and the approximant [ʋ]: after i and e usually [v], after u and o usually [w], at the start of a word and after a either (Elbert & Pukui 1979); the speaker of Parker Jones (2018) used only [v]
/l/ is a clear lateral, with a tap [ɾ] as a variant, mostly on other islands
the glottal stop between vowels is mostly realised as creaky voice without full closure
/p k/ are unaspirated in the traditional description; the revitalisation-generation speaker measured by Parker Jones (2018) aspirated them
short /a/ is [ɐ], and [ə] in function words; long /aː/ is more open; /a/ is closer before i and u in the diphthongs ai and au than in ae and ao
a glide [j] is inserted between i or e and a following vowel (mea), and [w] between u or o and a following vowel (nui)
consonants are rounded before rounded vowels; vowels are nasalised after nasal consonants
at the end of a phrase long vowels shorten and short vowels are devoiced
syllable_structure: (C)V(V): an optional consonant and a short vowel, a long vowel or a diphthong; no codas and no clusters
phonotactics: every word ends in a vowel; consonants never meet
vowel sequences that are not among the fifteen diphthongs are two syllables
clusters and consonants such as b, d, f, g, r, s, z occur only in unassimilated loanwords

stress.rule: Every syllable with a long vowel or a diphthong is stressed; the main stress is the last stress of the word, on the final syllable if it is heavy and otherwise on the penultimate syllable; in longer words the earlier stresses fall two or three syllables apart and are partly lexical (makuahine versus ʻelemakule).
stress.cues: pitch, duration and loudness; only short /a/ shows a quality difference

rhythm.vowel_reduction: moderate: short /a/ is centralised when unstressed or in function words; other vowels keep their quality
rhythm.notes: Schütz (1981) describes the rhythm in accent groups ('measures') of two or three morae. The mora-timed label follows the moraic stress system and the usual description of Polynesian languages; I know of no published rhythm metrics. At the end of a phrase long vowels are reported to shorten and short vowels to devoice, hence weak final lengthening.

length.notes: Long vowels and diphthongs count as two morae and are always stressed. Long and short /a/ differ in height (F1) as well as duration (Parker Jones 2018).

voice_onset_time_ms.source: Parker Jones 2018: one speaker of the revitalisation generation, read passage, six tokens of p and eight of k; older descriptions call the stops unaspirated

intonation.declarative: high on the first stressed syllables, then a gradual fall to low at the end
intonation.yes_no_question: same wording as a statement; the pitch stays high through the utterance and falls on the last stressed syllable, ending low (a falling question melody)
intonation.wh_question: not known to me in detail; treated by Murphy (2013), which I could not read in full
intonation.continuation: not known to me in detail; listing and continuation melodies are treated by Murphy (2013)
intonation.notes: The statement and yes-no question melodies follow Murphy (2013) and Elbert & Pukui (1979). The falling yes-no question is shared with Hawaiʻi Creole English.

phonation: creaky voice as the usual realisation of the glottal stop between vowels
devoiced short vowels at the end of a phrase

problems: the ʻokina is rendered as a short silence (phoneme _!) and not as a glottal stop or creak; at the start of a word it causes a long pause before the word and no consonant at all
w before a long vowel has no rule: wā and wō lose the w, and words such as uwē and ʻowā are spelled out letter by letter

the choice between [w] and [v] depends on the following vowel (v before i and e, w before a, o, u), whereas the literature conditions it on the preceding vowel: ʻewa, iwa, hewa come out with [w] where [v] is usual

a word with a long vowel gets its main stress on that vowel and no penultimate stress: mālama, kānaka, ʻōlelo are stressed on the first syllable instead of the penultimate; words with two long vowels get two equal main stresses
ae, ao, eu, oe, ou are two separate vowels; the long diphthongs are not defined
no devoicing or shortening at the end of a phrase
good: five short and five long vowels with a clear duration difference (about 120 against 300 units)
unaspirated p and k, as in the traditional description
ai, au, ei, iu, oi, ui are single diphthongs

notes: Parker Jones (2018) gives a formant plot but no table of values, so no formant block is given here.
